questions.stem: A 45-year-old nurse returned from voluntary work during an outbreak of Ebola virus in rural Guinea. She had been directly involved in caring for patients within the Red Zone (isolation area) in an Ebola treatment unit. Four days after her return she self-isolated and contacted her local public health unit as she had developed a fever, severe frontal headache, and a sore throat. Urine, serum, and an EDTA sample were sent urgently to the reference laboratory for an extended VHF PCR panel
questions.lead_in: What type of virus is Ebola classified as?
questions.explanation: Filovirus Ebola and Marburg are both filoviruses. They have a distinctive filamentous morphology under the electron microscope with a nonsegmented, negative-stranded RNA genome. They have a lipid envelope derived from host cell plasma membrane.

questions.model_answer:
a) Guinea, Liberia, and Sierra Leone (the unprecedented 2013-16 West African EBOV epidemic; 28,616 cases, 11,301 deaths).
b) 2 to 21 days (mean 4-10 days).
c) Patients are not contagious during the asymptomatic incubation period; infectivity begins with symptom onset and rises with viral load. Virus clears from blood on recovery but persists in immune-privileged sites (semen for months), permitting late sexual transmission.
d) Blood RT-PCR generally becomes positive around day 3 after symptom onset; a single early negative does not exclude disease and should be repeated (~72 h) as viral load rises to peak at days 3-10.
e) Sudden onset of fever with malaise and/or myalgia, followed by nonspecific features (may include an erythematous maculopapular rash, then GI symptoms and bleeding); labs show leukopenia/lymphocytopenia, thrombocytopenia, and elevated AST/ALT.
f) Family Filoviridae; genus Ebolavirus; species Zaire ebolavirus (EBOV).
questions.beyond_mandell: Timing of contagiousness and RT-PCR positivity/repeat testing are not stated in Mandell; from CDC/UpToDate Ebola guidance.

cohort_answer.text:
Countries affected: Sierra Leone, Guinea, Liberia. Currently DRC, Uganda
Incubation period: 2–21 days
Period of contagiousness: Patients are contagious only when they get symptomatic (not during the incubation period). Individuals who recover are minimally infectious during convalescence. Virus rapidly clears from the blood upon resolution of symptoms in survivors, although clearance is slower for immunologically protected sites, such as the kidney, gonads, and chambers of the eye. Virus can persist in semen for months after it has cleared from the blood. Thus, some level of sexual transmission of EV likely occurs. (CID)
PCR positivity: 3-10 days
Most common clinical presentation: Fever, severe headache, myalgia, fatigue, abdominal pain, and weakness followed several days later by vomiting, diarrhea, and sometimes unexplained bleeding or bruising. In kids, respiratory symptoms are more common and central nervous system manifestations are less common. A fleeting maculopapular rash on the torso or face after approximately 4 to 5 days of illness may occur.
Family, genus, species: Family: Filoviridae (RNA virus). Genus: Ebolavirus. Species: Zaire, Sudan, Bundibugyo, Tai Forest, and Reston (current outbreak is from Zaire sp). Zaire was responsible for the Sierra Leone outbreak. The Sudan species was also first recognized in 1976, and in four outbreaks in Uganda and Sudan, case fatality rates have averaged 50 percent. The Bundibugyo species has been responsible for small outbreaks in Uganda and the adjacent DRC, while the Ivory Coast virus has caused one nonfatal case. The Reston virus does not cause disease in humans. Vaccine: rvsv-zebov (recombinant vesiculostomatitis virus – zebo virus) – ring vaccination (close contacts). Zmapp not being used anymore. Mab114 or regan-eb3 currently being used

questions.model_answer:
a) Direct contact of mucosal surfaces or broken skin (small abrasions/tears) with infected blood or body fluids, or by parenteral introduction (e.g., reuse of unsterilized needles/syringes, nosocomial contact); primary spillover is from animal reservoirs (fruit bats) and infected primates/bushmeat.
b) Only once symptomatic; infectivity increases with viral load. There is no transmission during the asymptomatic incubation period.
c) At least 72 hours after symptom onset — an early negative blood NAAT should be repeated at 72 h, because viral RNA may be undetectable in the first ~3 days of illness.
d) Airborne precautions (routinely reserved for aerosol-generating procedures) can be removed once such procedures are no longer being performed; standard/contact/droplet precautions continue until the patient is confirmed negative or Ebola is excluded.
e) The outbreak is declared over after 42 days (two maximal 21-day incubation periods) have elapsed since the last confirmed case tested negative twice / since last possible exposure, with continued surveillance.
questions.beyond_mandell: Repeat-testing window, airborne-precaution criteria, and the 42-day outbreak-over rule are from CDC/WHO guidance (not in Mandell); only transmission routes are Mandell-grounded.

questions.model_answer:
a) Ebolavirus is a filovirus (family Filoviridae) causing viral hemorrhagic fever, first recognized in 1976 in Zaire (DRC) and Sudan; fruit bats are the presumed reservoir with spillover to primates/humans. Spread is by contact of mucosa/broken skin with blood/body fluids and by parenteral routes; incubation 2-21 days. The largest epidemic was the 2013-16 West African outbreak (28,616 cases, 11,301 deaths).
b) Mainstay is intensive supportive care — blood volume, electrolyte balance, and organ support (ventilation, dialysis), which markedly improved survival in patients evacuated to the US/Europe. Experimental antivirals used in 2013-16 included the monoclonal-antibody pool ZMapp, small interfering RNAs, and the small molecules favipiravir and GS-5734 (remdesivir).
c) Pregnancy is associated with severe disease and poor fetal outcomes, including fetal loss/spontaneous abortion and pregnancy-related hemorrhage.
d) Detection of virus in blood/tissue or filovirus-specific antibody: reverse-transcriptase PCR, ELISA for filovirus antigen and IgM/IgG, immunofluorescent antibody tests, rapid point-of-care antigen tests, and (less commonly) immunohistochemistry, virus culture, and electron microscopy.
e) Zaire ebolavirus (EBOV) was the strain responsible for the 2013-16 West African outbreak.
questions.beyond_mandell: Fetal outcomes in pregnancy are not covered in this Mandell slice; from UpToDate/WHO.

cohort_answer.text:
Family: Filoviridae. Spread through direct contact with blood/body fluids, needle sticks, contaminated objects, contact with infected animals/bushmeat/bats, semen of recovered men. Incubation 2-21 days. Infectivity: vitreous >1y, semen up to >550 days. Presenting symptoms: Fever, severe headache, muscle pain, fatigue, vomiting and diarrhea after 3-6 days, weakness, abd pain, bleeding/bruising. Contact and droplet precautions, AIRBORNE if AGMP. Outbreak considered over after 42 days/2 incubation periods. Strain in most recent outbreak: Zaire. Transmission: mosquito (A aegypti/albopictus), vertical, sexual, blood transfusions
Supportive care. Experimental therapies: ZMapp (triple monoclonal antibodies), convalescent plasma, Remdesivir, Mab114, REGN-EB3. RCT showed early stoppage due to inferior outcomes in ZMapp and remdesivir (~15% increased mortality vs Mab114/REGN-EB3)
Growing evidence pregnancy linked to severe ebola virus disease -> increased risk of fetal loss, pregnancy related hemorrhage
Leukopenia, transaminase elevations, thrombocytopenia, coagulopathy c/w DIC. RT-PCR (single negative early doesn't exclude, repeat in 72h; peak VL days 3-7; seminal fluid positive for months). Serology (antigen capture ELISA IgM/IgG, best yield 3 wks after acquisition). IHC tissue analysis of autopsy specimens
Ebola-Zaire (West African outbreak); Ebola-Sudan virus; Ebola-Ivory Coast (Tai Forest); Ebola-Bundibugyo

a) Direct contact of mucosa/broken skin with infected blood or body fluids (with parenteral spread via contaminated needles); initial spillover from animal reservoirs/primates.
b) The 2013-16 West African epidemic affected Guinea, Liberia, and Sierra Leone; prior/other EBOV and SUDV outbreaks occurred in DRC (Zaire), Sudan, Gabon, Republic of Congo, and Uganda.
c) Filoviridae (genus Ebolavirus).
d) Zaire ebolavirus (EBOV).
e) 2 to 21 days (mean 4-10 days).
f) Only once symptomatic — not during asymptomatic incubation.

questions.beyond_mandell: Infectious-when-symptomatic, airborne-precaution trigger, and the 42-day outbreak-over rule are from CDC/WHO/PIDAC guidance, not this Mandell slice.

cohort_answer.text: A) Contact with animal reservoirs; secondary human-to-human via direct contact with bodily fluids. B) Previous outbreaks DRC, Uganda, Sudan; 2014-2016 Guinea, Liberia, Sierra Leone, Mali, Senegal; 2018 two outbreaks in DRC (Zaire strain); 12th outbreak DRC Feb 2021. C) Filoviridae; genus Ebolavirus has 5 species (Zaire, Sudan, Bundibugyo, Tai Forest, Reston). D) Zaire strain: ~29,000 total cases, 15,000 lab confirmed, 11,000 deaths; first outbreak in Guinea, Sierra Leone, Nigeria, Liberia, Senegal, Mali; ring vaccination with VSV-based vaccine effective in Guinea. E) 2-21 days (mean 6-12 days). F) Once symptomatic. G) CDC: no evidence of airborne transmission but theoretical aerosol risk with AGPs and rapid deterioration - always wear N95; PIDAC also if VHF pneumonia considered. H) 42 days (2 incubation periods) after last possible exposure to a confirmed case.

questions.model_answer:
Mumps: RNA; enveloped; no specific antiviral (supportive).
Measles: RNA; enveloped; no specific antiviral (vitamin A adjunct; ribavirin unproven).
Hepatitis B: DNA; enveloped; yes - nucleos(t)ide analogues (tenofovir, entecavir), peginterferon.
EBV: DNA; enveloped; no established antiviral (aciclovir/ganciclovir have limited activity).
Ebola: RNA; enveloped; yes - monoclonal antibodies (atoltivimab-maftivimab-odesivimab [Inmazeb], ansuvimab [Ebanga]).
Zika: RNA; enveloped; none.
questions.beyond_mandell: Only measles (RNA, enveloped, ribavirin unproven, Mandell p. 2116) is covered by this chapter; the other rows are from general virology and current IDSA/CDC therapeutics.

questions.question: Name three immune-privileged sites where Ebola virus persists.

parts.text: What are THREE immune-privileged sites where Ebola persists?

parts_raw.text: What are THREE immune privileged sites where Ebola persists.

questions.model_answer: (1) The eye — aqueous/vitreous humor (uveitis months to a year or more after recovery). (2) The central nervous system — cerebrospinal fluid (relapsing meningoencephalitis). (3) The male reproductive tract — semen/testes (RNA detectable for many months, enabling sexual transmission).
questions.beyond_mandell: Immune-privileged persistence sites are not covered in this Mandell slice; from UpToDate/CDC data on Ebola survivors.

questions.model_answer:
a) (1) Aqueous/vitreous humor of the eye (persistent uveitis). (2) Cerebrospinal fluid / CNS (late relapsing meningoencephalitis). (3) Semen / testes (persists for many months, enabling sexual transmission).
b) Remdesivir (GS-5734) is a monophosphoramidate nucleotide (adenosine) analog prodrug; intracellularly activated to its triphosphate, it is incorporated by the viral RNA-dependent RNA polymerase and causes delayed chain termination, inhibiting viral RNA synthesis.
questions.beyond_mandell: Persistence sites and remdesivir mechanism are not detailed in this Mandell slice (GS-5734 is named only as a therapeutic); mechanism/persistence from UpToDate/product data.

questions.question_raw: AM 16. List of viruses - name whether it is DNA/RNA, Enveloped/not, and name an antiviral used for treatment (not immunotherapy) (whole chart - 3): Measles, Mumps, EBV, Zika, Ebola, Influenza, Hepatitis B (and Coronavirus)

parts.text: Complete the virus chart

parts_raw.text: Complete the virus chart

questions.model_answer: a) Measles: ssRNA, negative-sense (Paramyxoviridae); enveloped; no specific antiviral (vitamin A supportive; ribavirin only anecdotal in severe/immunocompromised disease). Mumps: ssRNA, negative-sense (Paramyxoviridae); enveloped; no specific antiviral - supportive care. Epstein-Barr virus: dsDNA (Herpesviridae); enveloped; no proven antiviral (herpesvirus DNA-polymerase inhibitors such as acyclovir/ganciclovir reduce shedding but not disease). Zika: ssRNA, positive-sense (Flaviviridae); enveloped; no specific antiviral - supportive care. Ebola: ssRNA, negative-sense (Filoviridae); enveloped; no small-molecule antiviral of proven benefit (remdesivir studied; licensed agents are monoclonal antibodies, i.e., immunotherapy). Influenza: segmented ssRNA, negative-sense (Orthomyxoviridae); enveloped; neuraminidase inhibitors - oseltamivir, zanamivir, peramivir (or baloxavir). Hepatitis B: partially double-stranded circular DNA (Hepadnaviridae); enveloped; nucleos(t)ide polymerase inhibitors - entecavir, tenofovir (or interferon-alfa). Coronavirus: ssRNA, positive-sense; enveloped with club-shaped spikes; remdesivir/nirmatrelvir-ritonavir for SARS-CoV-2.
questions.beyond_mandell: Baloxavir and SARS-CoV-2-specific agents (remdesivir, nirmatrelvir-ritonavir) postdate/lie outside this chapter; per IDSA influenza 2018 and IDSA COVID-19 guidance.

cohort_answer.text: Measles - Paramyxoviridae, ssRNA(-), enveloped: nothing (ribavirin trialed in severe cases, vitamin A). Mumps - Paramyxoviridae, ssRNA(-), enveloped: nothing. EBV - Herpesviridae, dsDNA, enveloped: nothing (GCV, cidofovir tried). Zika - Flaviviridae, ssRNA(+), enveloped: nothing. Ebola - Filovirus, ssRNA(-), enveloped: remdesivir, or Ervebo vaccine. Influenza - Orthomyxoviridae, ssRNA(-), enveloped: Oseltamivir/zanamivir/baloxavir. Hepatitis B - Hepadnaviridae, partially ds/partly ss circular DNA, enveloped: tenofovir, lamivudine, entecavir. Chikungunya - Togaviridae, ssRNA(+), enveloped: no Rx. Coronavirus - positive sense ssRNA, enveloped with club-shaped spikes.

questions.model_answer:
a) (1) Cerebrospinal fluid / CNS — meningoencephalitis can occur months after initial diagnosis, with infectious virus recovered from CSF. (2) Aqueous humor of the eye — uveitis presenting 1-2 years after infection. (3) Seminal fluid — virus persists for over a year, enabling sexual transmission.
b) Remdesivir (GS-5734) is a nucleotide (adenosine) analog prodrug; after intracellular conversion to its active triphosphate it is incorporated by the viral RNA-dependent RNA polymerase and causes delayed chain termination, blocking viral RNA replication.
questions.beyond_mandell: Persistence sites and remdesivir mechanism are not detailed in this Mandell slice; from UpToDate/product data.

cohort_answer.text: Patients can develop late manifestations after recovering from the initial illness. CSF - meningitis has occurred months after initial diagnosis (infectious virus recovered in CSF). Aqueous fluid - uveitis can occur 1-2 years after initial infection. Seminal fluid - persisted for over 1 year.
